questions.question: What is the difference between aggregation and composition in OOP?
options: They are identical relationships with different names

Composition is a strong 'has-a' relationship — the contained object's lifetime depends on the container (destroyed together); aggregation is a weak 'has-a' — the contained object can exist independently of the container
Aggregation means inheritance; composition means containment
Composition uses pointers; aggregation uses value members
questions.answer: Composition is a strong 'has-a' relationship — the contained object's lifetime depends on the container (destroyed together); aggregation is a weak 'has-a' — the contained object can exist independently of the container

Shallow copy nulls the source; move does not

questions.question: What is the significance of marking a destructor as 'noexcept' in C++?

noexcept on a destructor makes it virtual automatically
noexcept on a destructor prevents the object from being deleted
questions.answer: Destructors are implicitly noexcept by default in C++11 — if a destructor throws during stack unwinding (another exception already active), std::terminate() is called; marking it explicitly noexcept enforces this contract and enables optimizations

A static member is created inside each object just like instance members

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy problem and a double-free error?
options: They are unrelated issues with no connection

They are related: shallow copy causes two pointers to own the same heap memory; when both objects are destroyed, both call delete on the same address — the second delete is a double-free, which is undefined behavior often causing crashes or heap corruption
Double-free only occurs with delete[], not delete
Shallow copy always causes a memory leak, not a double-free

questions.question: What are the differences between public and private inheritance in C++?
options: public and private inheritance are identical

public inheritance models IS-A — base's public/protected members remain public/protected in derived (polymorphism works); private inheritance models IMPLEMENTED-IN-TERMS-OF — all base members become private in derived, and base* cannot point to derived (no polymorphism)

public inheritance makes all base members public regardless of their original access
questions.answer: public inheritance models IS-A — base's public/protected members remain public/protected in derived (polymorphism works); private inheritance models IMPLEMENTED-IN-TERMS-OF — all base members become private in derived, and base* cannot point to derived (no polymorphism)

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'has-a' and an 'is-a' relationship in OOP and how are they implemented in C++?
options: Both are implemented using inheritance in C++

IS-A is modeled by public inheritance (Dog IS-A Animal); HAS-A is modeled by composition or aggregation — a class contains another class as a member (Car HAS-A Engine); choosing correctly affects design correctness and polymorphism
HAS-A is modeled by multiple inheritance
IS-A and HAS-A are interchangeable design choices with no practical difference
questions.answer: IS-A is modeled by public inheritance (Dog IS-A Animal); HAS-A is modeled by composition or aggregation — a class contains another class as a member (Car HAS-A Engine); choosing correctly affects design correctness and polymorphism
